JAMES BAY HYDROELECTRIC PROJECT-ENVIRONMENTAL AGREEMENT-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to seek the consent of the House for a motion of urgent and pressing necessity brought about by the revelation by Mr. Andre Langlois, director of planning and development of the James Bay Development Corporation, who testified the other day in the injunction proceedings in the Superior Court in Quebec that on November 24 an agreement was signed by the Minister of the Environment on behalf of the federal government with the James Bay Development Corporation with respect to environmental matters. In light of yesterday's decision by the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development to have tabled before that committee correspondence between the federal government and the government of Quebec about the proposed James Bay development, and also the invitation to Premier Bourassa to appear before that committee, I would like to move the following motion pursuant to Standing Order 43 in order to have everything in one place:
That the agreement between the government of Canada and the James Bay Development Corporation dated November, 1972, relating to the environment in the area of the proposed James Bay hydro electric project be tabled.

subsubtopic: CMHC-INSULATION MATERIALS AND EXPERIMENTAL HOUSING
speechtext:
1.	Has consideration been given to the feasibility of altering CMHC specifications for the construction of dwelling units to increase the amount of insulation materials required in these dwellings to offset the shortage of fossil fuels and the tendency of the cost of fossil fuels to rise?
2.	What studies have been made by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the National Research Council in connection with house insulation specifications?
3.	What is the nature of experimental homes being constructed under the Housing and Urban Development Agency and what are the evaluations of these experiments?
[Mr. Nystrom.)

speakeroldname: Hon. Ron Basiord (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: CMHC-INSULATION MATERIALS AND EXPERIMENTAL HOUSING
speechtext:
1.
A proposal to increase the amount of insulation required in the construction of dwelling units has been prepared by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for consideration by the Associate Committee on the National Building Code.
2.	Studies on the requirements for insulation of housing have been carried out by the National Research Council, with the following reports having been published: (a) Determining Optimum Thickness of Insulation for Heated Buildings, NRC 8151. (b) Insulation Thickness for Houses, HN 21. (c) Insulation for Northern Buildings, NRC 5280. (d) Insulation of Houses, NRC 1386. (e) Thermal Insulation in Housing, CBD 16. (f) Insulation of the Home, BB2.
3.	The experimental houses built under the sponsorship of the Housing and Urban Development Association of Canada, with financial support from C.M.H.C., are designed with the object of testing new materials and techniques in home construction in the field. The major items tested in nine experimental projects to date have been prefabricated concrete foundation, plastic piping, water recycling equipment, pressure tested wood foundation, steel construction, reduction in size and number of structural components, new types of roofing, and new heating system designs. The program has involved the Association's local chapters in research activities, as well as manufacturers of components. The performance of materials and techniques in these projects is monitored by the Association in order to identify possible areas for experiment to be followed into the future. Grants totalling $133,000 have been approved by C.M.H.C. under Part V of the National Housing Act to assist in financing the construction of these experimental houses, and in monitoring the results. In addition, the construction of a number of these houses has been financed by NHA loans which have totalled $139,600.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: TREASURY BOARD-EVALUATION REPORT ON DIP
speechtext:
1.
There was a draft report prepared by the Treasury Board Secretariat that summarized the preliminary results of some econometric tests of one aspect of several industrial incentive programs, including the Defence Industry Productivity Program (DIP). This draft report did not seek to assess whether or not the benefits of these industrial incentive programs, in terms of their impact on the realization of the government objectives, warranted the costs incurred in carrying them out. The draft report was dated

March 14, 1973

February 9, 1973. Responsibility for the evaluation of the effectiveness of programs is borne by individual departments. If such delegation did not take place there would be either massive duplication, because the Treasury Board Secretariat would require almost as much technical expertise as departments now have, or the ministers responsible for particular programs would not have the kind of advice they need if they are to propose program changes designed to realize the government's objectives more effectively. The Treasury Board Secretariat has three functions to perform in so far as program evaluation is concerned: i. it carries out particular program evaluations as case studies for the purpose of demonstrating what kinds of evaluations can be achieved; ii. it develop* evaluative techniques that are applicable in assessing a whole range of programs; iii. it seeks to ensure that departmental evaluations of programs that affect the same objectives are carried out on a comparable basis so that interprogram comparisons can be made. Program evaluation is a continuous process within individual departments providing a flow of information to ministers and deputy heads on the extent to which government objectives are being affected by programs and of the changes overtime in the unit cost of producing particular program outputs. Therefore, it should not be inferred from the fact that a Treasury Board Secretariat evaluation report of a particular program does not exist that it is not being evaluated. Virtually every department in government now has the resources to carry out evaluations of the efficiency of its operations and the cost effectiveness of its programs.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege and I raise this point under Standing Order 17(1) which says that whenever any matter of privilege arises it shall be taken into consideration immediately. There is a second paragraph to Standing Order 17 which requires an hour's notice, unless the point of privilege relates to something that arose during the course of the sitting. The point on which I rise is something that did arise during the course of the sitting this afternoon. Indeed, it came up during the question period, but I felt that it was not proper to take time out of the question period by raising a point of privilege then, so I waited until the question period was over.
I realize that Your Honour has spent many hours pouring over the question of privilege, and we frequently have quoted to us the citation which says that members raise many points which really are not points of privilege. But I submit that in Beauchesne there is a clear statement that insults to members are to be regarded as a matter of privilege. I feel, Sir, that the House has been insulted todav by statements made by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) in answer to questions that were put to him. Yesterday, in answer to questions, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration very clearly said that the directives that were under discussion had been dispatched to the directors general of the manpower offices, and that they were to be taken in context with other regulations and other manuals or instructions. He also said that those directives were to be related to the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
This was not a chance, off-the-cuff, remark. It was clear yesterday, in the words of the minister, that the priorities that we had discussed related to manpower offices in giving priority to certain persons for available jobs. Today, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration says that some kind of a misunderstanding occurred last December, not between yesterday and today, but as of last December there was a misunderstanding and that all of this had to do with LIP grants.
I submit that it is pretty close to an insult to the House to ask us to believe today that he knew last December that these priorities related to LIP grants, whereas yesterday the minister clearly said that they related to the operations of the manpower offices. The minister made it clear yesterday that these directives had not been secret, and he said that they were to be taken into account after the normal operations required by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
I am not arguing whether the use of these directives was as bad as was made out in the House yesterday, but I do think it is an insult to the House to tell us one day that these matters related to the manpower offices and the next day that since last December the minister knew that they related to the granting of moneys under LIP. Therefore, I feel that the matter should be considered. I believe the minister, himself, should have a much better oppor-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset that today I am experiencing some throat trouble, so if I speak in a very low key this afternoon I hope hon. members will understand.
Last Friday afternoon, in the three or four minutes before the adjournment, I had an opportunity to make a few remarks on the Export Development Act and the amendments which are before the House in the form of Bill C-3. I should like to take two or three minutes now to summarize what I said at that time. The purpose of the amendments is relatively simple, that is, to increase the share capital of the Export Development Corporation from $75 million to $125 million and to increase the ceiling on loans and guarantees from $800 million annually to $1.5 billion.
On the surface, these amendments seem rather straightforward but I raised a couple of issues last Friday and I want to talk about them further this afternoon. The main purpose of the Export Development Corporation, other than lending money to foreign companies or foreign countries to purchase equipment and supplies in Canada, is to insure Canadian firms against non-payment for exports by foreign buyers and to insure Canadian foreign investors when they invest in other countries. This type of insurance only takes effect when a private commercial company will not risk insuring a corporation.
I feel that the bill before us is oriented too much toward big business, the multinational corporation. If you look at the type of credits that have been extended by the Export Development Corporation over the last few years, you will find that most of the financial arrangements for insurance and so on have been with the huge multinational companies, many of which are controlled by Americans.
I pointed out the other day that there is a strange involvement between big government and big business, and this is borne out when you look at the board of directors. The chairman of the board of directors of the Export Development Corporation is Mr. J. F. Grandy, Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Also a member of the board is Mr. T. M. Burns, Senior Assistant Deputy Minister; Mr. G. K. Bouey, Governor of the Bank of Canada; Mr. P. Gerin-Lajoie, President of the Canadian International Development Agency and that progressive figure, Mr. S. S. Reisman, Deputy Minister of Finance; Mr. A. E. Ritchie, Under Secretary of State for External Affairs and so on. On the private sector side, we see four business representatives on the board of directors of the EDC-Mr. Paul Leman, President of the Aluminum Company of Canada; Mr. I. S. Ross, President,
March 14, 1973

Swan Wooster Engineering Company, Limited of Vancouver; Mr. R. D. Southern, President of Atco Industries, Limited of Alberta and Mr. A. H. Zimmerman, Vice-President of Noranda Mines.
There seems to be a very interesting correlation here between big business and the government bureaucrats and mandarins, and some very interesting things have developed as a result of this strange, or perhaps not so strange, alliance. We find for example that Mr. Paul Leman, President of the Aluminum Company of Canada, was appointed to the board of directors in October, 1969. Perhaps there is a conflict of interest, Mr. Speaker, between his activities and one of the credits given by EDC. The minister might like to comment on that later. Mr. Leman is still on the board of directors of EDC and page 24 of the 1970 annual report of the Export Development Corporation shows that a credit was given to his company. The country concerned was Argentina and the contract was signed on December 11, 1970; the amount of financing was $7,500,000. I would be interested to know whether the President of Alcan was at the meeting where this particular credit was approved and whether he was involved in the decision. If he was, Mr. Speaker, this is an obvious conflict of interest and I think the minister owes the House an explanation when he speaks later in this debate.
When I look at the names of the directors and consider the financing that has been arranged and the firms to which the money is going, I wonder whether the government takes all the risk with the taxpayers' money and the multinational corporations take none. This is not what I understand as a free enterprise system; this is the type of system which we sometimes call the system of socialism for the wealthy, for the large corporations. When these corporations go into the other countries they are assured that there is absolutely no risk; they know that they will be insured by the Export Development Corporation, which is funded by the taxpayers of this country. I consider this an area of serious concern. I believe that the Export Development Corporation should be oriented more towards small businesses than towards large business, as is the case at present. At present, before a company may qualify for assistance, the size of transactions involved must be substantial. That, I believe, must be changed. The Export Development Corporation should help small businesses of this country.

Export Development Act
trading possibilities in South America. Also, a number of ministers responsible for trade, industry and commerce, including the previous minister, have taken trading missions to South America for that very purpose. Prior to that, this activity had been indulged in when the present hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) was minister of industry, trade and commerce. It is in that regard, and in that vein, that I wish to address my remarks.
Not only has it been our policy to expand trade in Latin America; it has also been, as it was in the days of the government formed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and subsequently, the policy of our government to try and promote goodwill and perhaps political expectations of one variety or another in Latin America. The government, so far as I have been able to observe, has tried to promote this policy. However, it is clear that loans and extensions of credit are not granted from a purely economic motivation, otherwise why would it make loans to Pakistan, where the experience has not been entirely satisfactory, to say the least. Clearly loans and credit are extended on political, not economic, motivation. It is clear to me, as has been admitted by functionaries in the EDC, that the government of Chile in Latin America is being discriminated against in this regard. I will give precise details in a few moments.
I should like to point out that in days gone by, when Cuba was taken over by a new government by force of arms, the government of the day in this country did not discriminate against that government. I can well remember this because I happened to be parliamentary secretary to the then minister of industry, trade and commerce. It was made public recently by the late Mr. A. D. P. Heeney that great pressure was placed on the Canadian government at that time not to trade with Cuba. My colleague, the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings, has confirmed this to me. Nevertheless, Canada did not succumb to that pressure not to trade in strategic materials with the government of Cuba. Whenever the Cubans wished to buy anything, and whenever circumstances permitted credit being extended, they were accommodated. It is my understanding that the government of the United States had a great deal more respect for the government of Canada after it had stood up to pressure than was the case previously. This policy worked well.
It is well known that the present government of Chile is an extreme left-wing government, headed by Prime Minister Salvador Allende. He, at least, achieved his position after being democratically elected, which was not the case in the Cuban situation. It is equally well known that the government of the United States is a little unhappy about the government of Chile, and has exerted pressure in one way or another to try to do what it can to make the government of Chile somewhat less popular than it has been in the past. I would be surprised if the government of the United States has not attempted to put pressure on the government of this country, through the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), and asked us to restrict credit to Chile. The reason is obvious. There are two industries in Chile which can provide foreign exchange. One is the copper industry, which is not in a healthy position, I gather; the other natural resource

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
industry is the forest products industry. According to information at my disposal, some of those natural resources are now ready for harvesting and can provide foreign exchange for Chile.
It is equally clear that the government of Chile is in a difficult foreign exchange position and has difficulty paying loans. I think the record of the country's trading with Canada has always been very good in the past. However, apparently it is the desire of the Canadian government not to extend credit to Chile because of that country's currency difficulties and also, I suspect, as I have already mentioned, for other reasons. Apparently this government's motivation, at least in part may arise from wisnmg to einoarrass the government of Chile because of its political leanings. Apparently this is government policy, and I hope the minister will make some reply in this regard. I cannot see how this policy would please those in this House who sit to my left, and who are the allies of this government. I would not think it would be to their liking at all.
The illustration I have in mind concerns a rather large firm in the city of Woodstock, Ontario, known as Timber Jack. This firms deals in logging equipment, that is, in log rolling equipment, and enjoys extensive sales all over the world. In the past many of these sales have been financed in one way or another by the EDC. Last year the government of Chile presented this firm, Timber Jack, which is the subsidiary of a multinational corporation, Eaton, Yale and Towne, with the opportunity to bid on a $4 million order for certain timber skidders and logging skidders. Conversations had gone on with the EDC concerning financing. This happened some months before tenders were invited on the order. When the people of Timber Jack talked with the people of EDC, it was apparent that EDC was agreeable to making the loan. As I say, this took place some months before the final decision was made with respect to tendering.
In any event, when the final chance came forward to make the tender, EDC turned the financing down. The terms, roughly, were 10 per cent cash down, which Chile was quite prepared to pay, and the rest was to be paid off over a relatively short period in equal monthly installments. In our previous experience in dealing with Chile, the financial obligations that Chile had incurred were always paid on the line. I was requested by the company concerned to find out what I could concerning this failure to help in the financing of this project. I discussed the matter with officials of EDC and was informed that they were acting in accordance with government policy not to extend loans to Chile at present. Apparently this has been not only the policy of this government, but of other governments as well. They did not specify which ones. Consequently, the order was turned down.
In addition to the fact that an industry in my city lost a $4 million contract because of this attitude and the subsequent loss of employment, all of which is important, there is the more important fact of our future trading relations with Latin America. In this particular instance, I understand that Brazil in fact financed a subsidiary company of Eaton, Yale and Towne which makes somewhat similar equipment. In any event, I do not think that Chile was

done out of the equipment. It might just as well have come from Canada. For a long time companies in this country, multinational corporations or otherwise, have tried to provide good service to Latin American countries on commercial orders. It is my view that this may well affect Canada's image in the Andean pact countries of South America in general.
It is quite true that if we refused to finance Chile in this case while Brazil did so, it will make suspect our future negotiations concerning trade not only with Chile but perhaps other Latin American countries as well. Chile is a business risk. It is certainly an investment risk. However, Canada can well afford to look to the future by taking some commercial risk transactions. I am sure the minister knows that in the past the EDC has taken certain risks. While they have not worked out as successfully as hoped, I do not think that anyone objected because Canada's long range policy and political policy, or perhaps I should say foreign policy, were perhaps served by making these risk loans.
As I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks, Canada has been trying for a long time to break into the Latin American market. It has also been our policy to promote good relations with Latin America. This sort of activity is hardly calculated to do that. In fact, it has the opposite effect. Our good neighbour to the south does not particularly care for the government of Chile for its own good reasons and expects us to follow suit by taking discriminatory action against Chile. That is indeed unwise. I hope the minister will be persuaded to feel this way. It is often said there is a price on everything and certain risks are too costly. In other words, the game may not be worth the candle. This in no way affects making loans in southeast Asia where there are doubtful expectations.
In future, if governments of a left wing stripe are not popular with a certain government, such as that of the United States, Canada should not discriminate against those countries on that ground, even if risks are involved. The long-term objective of this country, certainly in the interest of trade and foreign policies, should be that we form good relations with Latin America, even if certain risks are involved. I suppose if there were some serious crisis in Chile, such as the earthquake they have had recently, we would be glad to provide assistance. I suppose that is a different case because that assistance would be freely provided. In this case, some repayment is involved.
The two policies seem thoroughly inconsistent. I hope the minister will encourage his colleagues in cabinet to reconsider their attitude with regard to trading with Chile, even though it may be against undoubted American pressures. I realize that our friends to the south are in a pretty strong bargaining position now, in view of the fact the auto pact is coming up for renegotiation. I hope the minister will give us a reply in this regard.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I look at the bill before us, I think the program, undertaken in the past several years by the Export Development Corporation, could make us wonder whether this bill should be under the aegis of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) because there are certain features of the EDC that suggest it is a "gravy train". It lends money to customers of Canadian corporations, but so often these are the big corporations. It insures Canadian corporations against non-payment by foreign producers, but so often these are the big corporations. It guarantees financial institutions against loss when they lend to corporations that may get into trouble overseas, but so often these are the big ones.
As of December 31, 1972, eight Canadian corporations shared 50 per cent of the benefits in EDC. If the outstanding offers that are before the corporations are accepted, the big eight share can go up to 64.8 per cent. This means that almost two-thirds of the money available for assistance to expand Canadian exports is being monopolized by eight major concerns. We ought not to jump to the conclusion that this, in itself, is bad. Bigness is not necessarily good, but it is not necessarily wrong either. None of us want to go as far as the former president of General Motors in the United States who said that he thought what was good for General Motors was good for the United States. I do not think we are inclined to go to that extreme and think that whatever is good for the "Big Eight" is also good for Canada. Neither do we want to draw the opposite conclusion that anything that is done to assist these corporations to develop and carry on business is necessarily bad for the people of Canada. We recognize that they employ Canadians and are putting something important into the economy for the development of this country. None the less, we should not jump to the other conclusion that we are giving the Canadian people the best assistance we can when we are giving this kind of encouragement to the major industrial corporations in Canada.
There are at least two points of criticism that can be offered under this heading. One fault with the way in which the finances of the EDC are being distributed is the way in which they involve an imbalance among the provinces of Canada. Five of the big eight are from one province and three are from another. We must give much more recognition to the need for a better distribution of finan-
Export Development Act
cial resources of EDC across the country in order to encourage the development of exporting industries in other parts of Canada.
However, we must give consideration as well to the way small businesses in Canada are being affected by the actions of EDC and its regulations under which a project must normally involve a minimum of $1 million. This reduces the chances of a small business enterprise getting into the export market with the help of the EDC. I think that parliament ought to give more consideration to improvements to EDC programs that would give priority to small businesses in this country. We are not questioning the principle of the EDC and we are not calling into question the fact that the EDC should be free to assist major exporters in the country, but we would like to see a re-examination of the priorities of EDC so that greater advantage can be given to small businesses, enabling them to develop the export dimension of their programs they have not been able to undertake.
So, we would ask that the minister in charge of this corporation, and the government generally, give consideration to this kind of critical question: Is sufficient publicity provided to small businesses describing the services available from the Export Development Corporation? It has been my experience in dealing with small businesses that very often those in charge are not always aware of the programs the government makes available. Very often they are quite uninformed about projects and programs the government has undertaken because these have not been fully explained. It would be of interest to the country if the department responsible for the EDC undertook a more energetic effort to reach out to small businesses in Canada to enlighten these people in order that they might participate in the export markets of the world with assistance from the EDC.
Second, I would ask this critical question: Is it the policy of the Export Development Corporation to avoid transactions which would, by the very nature of small businesses, discourage the use of its services? I can appreciate that it is often more simple for the EDC and other government agencies to deal with well-staffed and highly sophisticated corporations which operate on the level of government departments. We hear and witness all around us big government, and we can appreciate that big government is very much in tune with big business. What we would like to see is a conscious and sincere effort by the EDC to take cognizance of the small business firm and employer, reaching out to encourage him to become active in the export market.
Third, we would ask whether it is a policy of the government or that of the EDC that the small business corporation should be forced to go to the private lending institutions? One of the major problems faced by small business today is the lack of adequate capital. Anyone who deals with small businessmen today knows they are constantly challenged by the problem of finding enough capital with which to equip themselves and expand their markets. Very often they have visions of new markets they can penetrate. They have the energy and initiative with which to do so, but they lack equipment and staff because they lack capital. What they need is a positive, creative and

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
sincere effort by the government to assist them finding what they need most, and that is capital financing. If the EDC and the government of this country intend to help small business in Canada in the way required, they will have to do something such as this. They must consider establishing a branch of the EDC which will have as its prime concern and responsibility the provision and promotion of services to small businesses. If the government undertook this it would not only assist these businesses, but would go a long way toward meeting at least part of the unemployment problem in this country.
We are aware that one of the features of business life today is that small business tends to be labour intensive, to a much greater degree than big corporations which often can afford equipment that actually reduces the number of jobs provided in the past. If we want to increase jobs we have to increase the number of small businesses.
Even more important, we have to help small businesses to stay alive. It is often said that the greatest bankruptcy rate in business today occurs among the small entrepreneurs. This is because they lack adequate capital and other means of staying in business. That is why we want to put emphasis on the needs of some of the finest people in this country; people who are making a noteworthy contribution to their communities. They should receive much more in the way of incentives and support from the government than they have to date.
Such a small business branch of the EDC could assist and make efforts to improve the balance of payments position of Canada, because we would find small businesses participating in the export market, resulting in much greater diversification of products for overseas export. We are all conscious of the difficulties Canada has suffered for a long time because so much of our export trade has been directed to one country. The vast majority of our export products are going to the United States, and we must certainly diversify in terms of our customer countries. To do that we must look for new markets and develop new products available for export in a fashion that has not been followed in the past.
We plead with the government to think very seriously about the possibility of making a creative contribution to the economic expansion of this country by assisting that part of the economy which has for a long time lagged in export opportunities. Small business requires considerable assistance in this regard because a great deal of our difficulty in the export market relates to competition with other countries which have cheaper labour resources. We must assist small business to find ways to develop competitive programs rather than cheap labour resources. We must assist them to find better competitive methods in terms of improved efficiency of operation, improved products and greater quality in order that they will be more competitive. We cannot hope to accomplish this in terms of lower labour costs.
If small businesses are to make this kind of advance they will need the co-operation of the government, not the kind of handouts from Ottawa in the last few years which have gone to others as welfare help. We all believe that those who help themselves should be helped by others, and this is what we are asking for in this instance. We

believe in assistance to the small businessman who, with a limited operation, must undertake most of the administration and management on his own. He cannot afford the research departments or the promotional efforts or the great sales forces available to big business. That kind of person needs the help of the government to give him a chance to stay alive in our economy. So, we urge^ the government to make this a priority.
We should recognize that intentionally or not our smaller operations in Canada have suffered from a lack of available financial resources. I have already referred to their difficulty in finding adequate capital. For example, in 1964 the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance reported that one-third of Canadian-controlled companies with assets of under a million dollars had inadequate supplies of long term capital. This is still the case and unless we resolve the problem in a positive way an increasing number of small businesses will be obliged to quit their operations. They will be forced to sell out to big corporations and, as hon. members know, those big corporations are often subsidiaries or agents of multinational corporations. When we speak about the future of Canada, we cannot be serious when we talk about repatriating the economy unless we are serious about helping Canadian-owned small business institutions.
I would like to turn, now, Mr. Speaker, to another dimension of this topic. I wish to refer to the way in which the EDC has, in my opinion, not only an economic responsibility but a social responsibility to help the have-not peoples of the world to help themselves. I think the minister, in his opening address to this debate, conveyed the impression that the EDC finds some of its justification in doing just that. I agree with what he says. I think we should be impressed by many of the things that the EDC has made possible. It has enabled Canadians to sell to have-not countries equipment which has enabled them to develop their resources. We certainly agree with the EDC carrying out that kind of program. But, at the same time, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why he omitted to mention that the EDC was involved in the erection of a luxury hotel in the Caribbean.
I do not quite see how this fits in with the social aims of the Export Development Corporation. The ordinary taxpayers in Canada certainly cannot afford to go to this luxury hotel; the ordinary citizen in the Caribbean certainly cannot afford to do anything but work in that kind of institution. We must therefore wonder whether this is the best way to utilize the money being made available by the taxpayers of Canada to meet the needs of the ordinary citizens in Caribbean countries or elsewhere in the world. With regard to the particular enterprise to which I have just referred, I should like to know just how much Canadian content was involved. We read in the regulations of the EDC that the projects financed by EDC must contain 80 per cent Canadian content. Well, perhaps 80 per cent of the materials used in that hotel came from Canada. But it would certainly be interesting to learn whether that was so.
Another question I feel I must ask is why this kind of aid should be provided to countries which do not appear to have an obvious need for such facilities. For instance, I
March 14, 1973

look at countries such as France, Argentine, Brazil, to name just a few, and I wonder why there is a special need for Canadians to help finance their imports from this country. Perhaps there is a good answer to that, but it is not obvious and I think we should be concerned about not only the imbalance in the distribution of the funds of the corporation, chiefly among eight corporations and two provinces, but also to the assistance provided to countries where the need is not as great as could be found elsewhere.
A fundamental question of principle which I should like to raise before the House is this: is the program of the EDC really the best way to help advance the Canadian economy? Should we not recognize that many more jobs would be created if we were to help small business enter the export market and assist them to do so by granting them the kind of loans which the EDC has shared among the big eight? For example, if we compare the operations of the Industrial Development Bank, which does assist many small businesses in Canada, with the record of the EDC we find that the Industrial Development Bank is making money available at a much higher rate of interest than the EDC makes available to the much larger corporations. The average interest rate charged by the Industrial Development Bank in 1972 was 9.86 per cent. The rate charged by the Export Development Corporation was only 7 per cent. We might also wonder about the size of loans which the Industrial Development Bank makes available to some of our smaller companies in contrast to the size of loans available to our major corporations. The average size of loans made by the Industrial Development Bank in 1972 was in the order of $5,000. Those made by the EDC were $23.3 million.
Look at this from another standpoint, Mr. Speaker. Should we be doing more for the Canadian people if we concentrated on creating jobs in Canada and providing services in Canada with the funds that are available to the EDC? I think we have often leaped to conclusions when making judgments about exports and when making judgments about aiding industry. It has been thought that if we provide fast write-offs and other concessions we would be bound to create jobs. We have thought that if we expended exports we would be bound to create jobs. But so frequently this is not the case.
It has been remarked that generals are usually best at fighting old wars. This is not to be wondered at when one considers that so much of their time is spent in military colleges studying old wars. They are trained, very often, to consider how they might have won this battle or that campaign. They are taught to identify the mistakes made by generals in the past, and so on. Is this not equally true of economists? Often we look back some years, sometimes a generation, to this economic theory or to that economic theory. We become so wedded to the principles enunciated by one economist or another, principles which for a time had validity, that we forget that other changes in the lifestyle of the world have made those theories outdated. I would therefore suggest that some very critical questions be asked about the effectiveness of EDC in contributing to the expansion of the number of jobs in Canada as well as to enriching the life of the Canadian people.
Export Development Act
The point at issue here is whether the money we make available to assist our export trade should be used just to permit our larger corporations to increase their record for any particular year. We ought to be dovetailing our export program in with our whole concern for solving unemployment, our whole concern for expanding the number of jobs available to the Canadian people, our whole concern for putting more purchasing power into the hands of the Canadian consumer. When we can provide a clear, firm and positive resolution of these concerns then there is full justification for the EDC program. Until this is the case, I think we must critically examine the whole proposition.
Very often the economic policies of the government remind me of a group of church women who went out selling tickets to a church supper. They were asked by a man to whom they tried to sell tickets: "Why do you want to sell tickets?" They told him they were putting on a church supper. "Why do you put on a church supper?" was his next question. "Well, we want to raise funds", they replied. To his inquiry as to why they wished to raise funds they said: "In order to pay for the hall we have built". "Why did you build the hall?" he asked. "In order to have a place in which to hold the supper".
There is a kind of circular uncritical assumption about many economic policies that are very much like that circular uncritical effort of those particular women. I think the time has come, not simply in respect of this one but many other major programs of the government, to ask to what extent these programs are making a major contribution to the achievement of Canada in reducing unemployment, giving people an opportunity to support themselves, and giving Canadian entrepreneurs and businessmen an opportunity to develop the resources of this country in conjunction with the working people of this country. If we were to ask that kind of question I think we might very well find that we would be doing more for the Canadian people were we to make some changes in the efforts of the EDC. We might very well find that if we put some federal money into the provision of better transit in some of the major population centres of the country we would do more to create jobs for Canadian people and provide services for the Canadian people than by shipping certain products across the sea.
We must ask ourselves what our priorities are. We must ask what the best way is to meet the human needs of the Canadian people. Then, we must ask whether the EDC is achieving this. Finally, I should like to call the attention of the House to the need for parliament, the government and this corporation, which is our under authority, to give greater help to Canadian-owned industries. One reason for helping small businesses is that very often they are Canadian-owned, certainly to a far greater degree than is the case among the major corporations. When we face the fact that EDC is giving priority to these major corporations many of which are foreign controlled and are subsidiaries then we must become increasingly critical because most of the capital of EDC is going in this direction. Of 43 firms which benefit from EDC, 21 are foreign-controlled. We are given the impression that this program is yet another way to really help this country be controlled

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
and indeed owned by foreign interests, particularly United States interests.
Indeed, we must be increasingly concerned about the fact that EDC is another government agency that is feeding the expansion or dominance of the world by multinational corporations. In looking over the report of the EDC, one might wonder whether very often in its program it is financing one branch of a multionational corporation to buy from a Canadian branch of the same corporation. We must therefore have increasing concern about the way in which EDC, and along with it the private lending institutions of this country, should be required or at least encouraged to give greater priority to Canadian-owned companies.
When we talk about the repatriation of our country's economy we should be more concerned with that than we have been even about the repatriation of our constitution. We must recognize that very frequently government programs are contributing to the alienation of Canadian control. So, we ask again that the government re-examine the program of the Export Development Corporation with a view to giving priority in terms of financing and other aid to Canadian-owned institutions. It is not that we are suggesting they should not make assistance available to any firm that is operating within Canada and for the interest of Canada, but we would like a greater priority given to those companies which are 100 per cent Canadian.
For these reasons, we would call on the government to adjust its priorities. We would ask that it give greater priority to small businesses, to give greater priority to parts of the country which do not have sufficient industrial development, to give greater priority to labour intensive businesses which are seeking assistance and to give greater priority to Canadian-owned companies as well as to the social need abroad and the social need at home. When those priorities are taken seriously by the corporation and by the government then we certainly can be 100 per cent in support of the aims and objectives of the EDC. Until then, we must remain critical of it in the interest of the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate and to follow my distinguished and learned colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse), who I think has brought out a significant number of home truths when we consider this bill as being, as it is, part of the whole economic posture of the government and indeed the economic posture of our country. It is too bad, I suppose,- perhaps it is not really-that we are considering this bill only in the light of increasing the capital of the corporation because the problems which face us go far beyond the simplicity of the text of the statute. However, perhaps in some respects it is fortunate, if the present situation can be called fortunate, that we consider this matter on a day when we have had the release by Statistics Canada in respect of the actual rate of unemployment in our country which stands at the appalling level of 7.3 per cent of the work force, and wnen we realize tnat we are considering this bill at a time when there are 655,000 Canadians out of work.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) speaks of unemployment in human terms. I think the hearts of every

member on both sides of the House go out to those 655,000 people many of whom, perhaps most of whom are still, for some reason or another, unable to find jobs. When we speak about this bill in the context of the discussion in this House, and witness the apparent confusion in the Department of Manpower and Immigration, it is evident that the government takes no joy from this situation or from the fact that the unemployment rate is down ever so slightly. It certainly is nothing to write home to mother about. I am sure they take no joy-nor do we because we go further and condemn them-in respect of the economic policies which place our country and our young people in a position where they are potentially one of the groups with the highest unemployment level in the world among young people. I think this is very serious, having regard to what this means to them and their view of what our country could do for them.
I believe we are hampered to a great extent in judging the economic impact which this simple amendment will have by the fact that the Minister of Finance of this country, let alone the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie), who has been stung by the mistakes of his 1972 budget and has repeated them again in his 1973 budget, still fails to tell us what projection he would make with regard to the generation of employment. It is difficult to consider this bill, which deals with the export affect on our economy, without knowing where the Minister of Finance stands.
This government chose to remain in office; it chose to cling to office or, as that sign says, to "hang in there, baby", or whatever you want to say. They had every constitutional right to do that, but in so doing-and I think there is a quid pro quo in this-there was to be an offering in return for the confidence of the House of some economic programs for the development and health of the economy of our country which would be of some real significance, but there have not been any. As we look at this bill today, one that is as important as this one with respect to the industrial development of our country, we find that there is still nothing significant in it.
Instead of this government coming to the House merely asking for an increase in the share capital of this corporation, I would rather have had the government come to the House to answer the questions that are on the lips of the army of unemployed in our country. I would like this government to give answers to those who have to support those unemployed. I would like the government to give real, substantial tax relief, and not be afraid to back it up by saying that this is where the tax relief will function in the economy and such will be the results. I would rather have had this government come before the House with policies of economic expansion, new policies on transportation, real help for pensioners, and perhaps the beginnings of justice for public servants. But instead, we are being asked to approve merely an increase in the share capital of an important corporation, and the minister has not given us any indication of how this fits into the whole economic package which the government wishes the Canadian people to believe it has. I think this is important.
March 14, 1973

The Export Development Corporation was formed in October of 1969 to help develop markets abroad for Canadian exporters. The concept was a good one and it is still a good one. I think it is essential for Canada to support the concept because Canada, for better or worse-and sometimes one wonders about that-is one of the world's great trading nations. I suggest to you, Sir, that much more is needed in this amendment than merely to increase the ceiling. I suggest to you that the whole concept of the bill must be looked at in depth. It may be that the ceiling which the government seeks to increase is not high enough and that a complete review of the operations of the corporation might be the answer. However, this debate will not supply that kind of review.
It may be that in the course of this review we would find out, not only that the amendment is deficient in terms of the amount of the increase requested, but that our whole approach to resource development must be reconsidered. It may very well be that our banking policy may also have to be reviewed. There is nothing here about that important aspect. It may be that our research and development policies should be reconsidered and I commend to members of the House the testimony of Dr. Schneider, chairman of the National Research Council, before the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates a few days ago, with respect to the importance of research and development and whether it is being neglected, negligently or deliberately.
Perhaps out of such a review-and I wish we could have this review-we would come forward with some new policies with respect to transportation so that the patchwork quilt of policies which have been ours for so many years may be reshaped. Perhaps we could rethink and redirect the whole work of the Industrial Development Bank and its role in the scheme of things. I think this is possible. Probably we should take a good honest look for once and hear some honest comments from the government on the significance of the DISC program in the United States to see how it really affects us. I think that, in the course of that review, we would be able to look at our tariffs and we could come to grips with the whole sorry mess of foreign ownership and foreign investment in this country. In short, rather than applying another economic bandaid- and this is all this bill is-this review would have been much more meaningful to the House, for the government, and the Canadian people.
Some of my colleagues have spoken about small business. Canada has become dependent on one market which takes up about two thirds of our export trade. The bulk of our sales is in such primary fields as forest products, mining, oil and gas. If you look at the statistics, you will find that there is comparatively little in the manufacturing field other than the trade resulting from the auto pact. There is no doubt that large corporations dominate the export field. In 1970, 87 corporations with sales of over $25 million accounted for almost 70 per cent of Canadian export sales, and 426 exporters executed 92 per cent of the exports reported.
I think it is important that we note that the EDC provides financing for initial terms of 12 to 15 years at average interest rates of 7 per cent, and eight countries have received 59 per cent of the money, Mexico being the
Export Development Act
largest with $130 million. In the past year, the EDC concluded long-term, five to 15 year financing agreements with foreign buyers totalling $283 million. At the end of the year they had over $1 billion in outstanding long term contracts. As a result of these statistics and this evidence, weaknesses in the EDC's approach are now becoming apparent. Their activity appears-and I say this with great respect-to be encouraging rather than discouraging the concentration of our trade, particularly with respect to individual exporters. This is a decided weakness.
A review of this $1 billion financing reveals that 50 per cent of it benefited only eight Canadian exporters, four of whom are subsidiaries of American concerns. On average, these companies have received or are receiving $64 million each in export finance benefits. The largest is the Montreal Engineering Company Limited which has some $101 million in benefits. I am not suggesting that those things, by themselves, are wrong, but I am suggesting that the efforts, the energy and the funds have become too centralized in too small an area and that many Canadian small businesses and the potential of small businesses have been ignored.
The Export Development Corporation is not fulfilling its role as we had anticipated, and we in this party believe that the EDC should assist small businesses to enter this field and should favour-in fact, I am prepared to use the word "prefer"-Canadian small business and Canadian-owned corporations as opposed to foreign subsidiaries. Last year, for example, of those identifiable only 13 Canadian exporters benefited from the $283 million in long-term financing provided by EDC. Out of those 13, nine were foreign subsidiaries. These are pretty important statistics.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: And thousands of Canadian suppliers, small part suppliers.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: I appreciate the interruption from the minister. I am not suggesting that thousands of suppliers did not benefit. I think this is a misinterpretation of what I said. All I am saying, and I think most members of the House will agree, including those who support the minister, is that at this time, in the context of our own economic situation in this country, an emphasis ought to be put upon the development of Canadian-owned small business.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
And, Mr. Speaker, there ought to be a review of the operations of the EDC to see if a concentration has not, inadvertently or otherwise, taken place with respect to its operations that has resulted in the defeat of what I think is a generally acceptable Canadian objective.
My colleague from Scarborough East mentioned the work and undertakings of the Industrial Development Bank, and how it has, in fact, gone the other way. The Industrial Development Bank has been a fine example, in terms of concept in any event. I have some question about some of the terms and conditions under which it grants loans because its failure rate indicates either very astute investors or else the fact that the bank is not taking many

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
risks. This Industrial Development Bank has assisted over 16,000 customers who borrow small amounts of money for the purposes set forth in that statute. It is doing a good job. I think the use of the Industrial Development Bank by Canadian businessmen is significant, compared with the rather centralized thrust of the Export Development Corporation. That is a statistical fact.

Surely, the support for these small-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I enjoyed listening to the minister's speech earlier, but I do not want to have to listen to a second speech now.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext: Are you aware of that fact?

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Of course, I am aware of it. It is contained in the report of the corporation, but it is only one part of the potential operation of the corporation. My point, Mr. Speaker, is that the government is really looking only at a very small aspect of the problem when it comes to this House and asks the House to increase the share capital of the corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: We are doing more than that, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Our concern with the Export Development Corporation is with its failure-it may be a failure in good faith, if there is such a thing-to harness its full potential. Our concern lies in the realization of what the Export Development Corporation can do as compared with what it has done.
As hon. members in all parties have said, there is no doubt that the chronic problem of Canadian business is the shortage of capital. My hon. friend from Scarborough East mentioned the advice given by the Royal Commission on Banking and Finance in 1964. A more recent picture is given by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce study called "Foreign Owned Subsidiaries in Canada, 1964-49." It examines the operations of all foreign held non-financial corporations in Canada with assets of more than $5 million.
In 1969, the last year of the study, these corporations reported net external funds of $353 million. Of this amount, $204 million came in the form of Canadian bank loans. What this means is that for the year 1969 nearly two-thirds of the money used in these transactions came from Canadian banks, and the total owed at the end of 1969 was $1.17 billion. I believe that the Export Development Corporation is guilty of the same bias. A large

percentage of its funding and its energy has been given to foreign controlled firms.
In the past year, the EDC signed long-term financing agreements with foreign buyers totalling $283 million. At the end of the year it had over $1 billion in outstanding long-term contracts. A review of that $1 billion, as I said, reveals that 50 per cent of it benefited only eight Canadian exporters, four of which are subsidiaries of American concerns. In sum I think it is fair to say that the government has helped large American-owned corporations retain control of the export business in Canada. That may not be what it intended, but that is the net effect of what has happened.
I think that a better case than the government has made could be made for putting $1.5 million of public money into the EDC. If foreign firms, most of them American, continue to get first crack at the loans of the Export Development Corporation, Canadian firms are thereby denied. Canadian manufacturers would like to become more active in the export field, but in terms of quantum they really get little help from the EDC. This is a sad state of affairs. I want you to understand, Mr. Speaker, that we are not calling for discrimination against foreign controlled firms, but as the hon. member for Scarborough East said, we are calling for a re-evaluation of our priorities as Canadians. Canadians will never benefit from any position of narrow nationalism. But that is not to say that a Canadian government or a Canadian parliament ought not to hold that it is worthy of it to recognize the needs of the Canadian business community.
In recognizing the needs of the Canadian business community, it is my respectful submission that we will also keep our eye on those 665,000 unemployed, that we will not forget that there is 7.3 per cent of Canadian workers out of work, that the object of the government, whether we are dealing with the EDC or otherwise, ought to be to use its best efforts to promote the development of Canadian small business, which is the greatest employer in this country, and that we ought to create in this country an atmosphere where Canadian business can do its own thing, as opposed to the government entering the field and doing the same thing for business people. I believe that this ought to be the proper thrust of this legislation, and not just of this legislation but of everything that is considered by this parliament. Finally, Mr. Speaker, we ought to reconsider the allocation of additional funds unless a Canadian preference approach is adopted by this corporation.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing here with a bill to amend the capital structure of the Export Development Corporation by increasing the advances to that corporation from $850 million to $1.5 billion. I am sure most members of the House of Commons are desirous of giving every assistance to business in this country to export its products. If it were that simple, the House would have passed Bill C-3 some time ago but of course it is not. The bill gives the House an opportunity to re-examine the Export Development Corporation, to consider its annual report and financial statement and its performance.
March 14, 1973

It becomes apparent that the corporation is involved with 43 companies; eight of them are major companies which have half the money now and pretty soon will have 64 per cent or 65 per cent of it. The corporation also has a fancy list of directors and a beautiful prospectus with pictures in four or five colours. One begins to wonder why a company with only 43 customers, eight of them major, has to spend money on offices in Ottawa and branches in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal, why it wants $11 billion so that it can use 64 per cent of that amount to service eight companies! Mr. Speaker, four of these companies are owned by shareholders in another country.
The hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse) raised the question of priorities and I shall comment on that later. Some time ago when I was analysing the question of export development, I asked some businessmen in Mississauga what assistance they received from the federal government with regard to foreign trade. One of them, and I will be glad to give the minister the name of the company, told me, "We don't get any help from Ottawa. The only place you can get help for trade in this country is from the province of Ontario because the province at least is concerned about small business. We are not a big company, we only make wheel barrows and concrete buggies but the province of Ontario made it possible for us to get going and we are now selling to Peru and other places." What is wrong with this government, Mr. Speaker, that it even permits the provinces to get involved in foreign trade? The trouble is that this government, and this minister, are not doing an adequate job. In many cases, small business has to look to the provincial minister of trade for assistance. I ask the minister, Mr. Speaker, is this the way our export trade should be developed? Is this government only interested in the big, the powerful, the foreign-owned?
Some hon. members have said that we are really not concerned about the fact that some of the loans have been made to foreign corporations but, Mr. Speaker, we are concerned about the proportions and we are concerned that the interests of Canada and Canadian businessmen take second place in the deals that are organized. It seems that it is easier for the Export Development Corporation to deal with a few large companies than with small companies. It is one of the tragedies in Canada today that these few large companies are foreign-owned. It is easier to deal with them because they know what it is all about- they know the game. They can afford to send their lackeys to Ottawa; they can afford to stay in the fine hotels and entertain members of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce; they can afford to fight their way through the maze of government offices; they can afford to calculate how to qualify on a project and they know that this government is prepared to play ball with them and is spending great amounts of money. How many customers are serviced by these great amounts of money, Mr. Speaker; just 43?
A lot has been said about small business, Mr. Speaker, and I want to point out that through the Industrial Development Bank assistance is available to small business at an interest rate pretty close to ten per cent. I want to point out, too, that the Export Development Corporation is prepared to lend money to large companies at 7 per cent so that they can finance foreign trade. How can we justify
Export Development Act
treating the small businessman like this when he has contributed so much to the development of Canada? He cannot afford to lobby or entertain, but he pays 10 per cent and the big corporations pay 7 per cent. This is the kind of thing we are concerned about.
