speechtext: Is the hon. member aware that the loan is made to the buyer and not to the seller? There is no loan to the Canadian customer; it is made to the foreign buyer.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: That is very interesting. I am delighted that the minister has pointed out that he is prepared to lend to Canadian businessmen at 10 per cent and to foreign businessmen at 7 per cent. That is the kind of attitude we expect from this government.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: You hanged yourself there, Alastair. Any other gems?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext: Well, he hasn't got it straight yet.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this corporation compares to some extent to a corporation in the United States called the Export-Import Bank. That corporation has a different method of operation to some extent because it does not put up all the money but only a portion of it, approximately 30 per cent, and approaches the private sector for the balance. We have pretty significant and large private banks in Canada. Indeed, the Royal Bank of Canada and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, in terms of size and capital structure, rank high among the world's banks. It seems strange to me, and to other members on this side of the House, that only some $20 million has been supplied by Canadian banks and that the balance of the finances of this corporation come directly from this government. I think one can say this: this corporation is being lazy. It is not going onto the street and looking for the money with which to finance exports in the normal course. It finds it easier to take money from the taxpayer and make long-term loans with its own money. It does not operate as a bank or exchange department; it operates the easy way, by sitting back and using its own money. When it runs out of money, it comes crying to parliament for more. It could easily go to the various chartered banks of this country and work out some insured loan participation arrangement; but it is easier to operate as it now does.
Perhaps the reason for its actions is that it insists on lending money at rates lower than those used by the banks; perhaps that is why large foreign corporations and multinational corporations of reputation come to this government for financial assistance. The financial assistance available here is perhaps cheaper than credit assistance available anywhere else. I suggest that multinational corporations know how to look after imports and exports and sales from one branch to another. Perhaps the whole organization of this corporation needs overhauling, since it seems that the foreign business community and large corporations are treating this government and this development corporation as an easy mark.
In our examination of this bill we should be examining the entire principle behind the establishment of the Export Development Corporation. We should know exact-

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
ly how it is operating on behalf of the Canadian people. If the Export Development Corporation and the government wish to demonstrate that they are not wedded to the idea of assisting only large corporations, I suggest they should consider establishing a department within the corporation whose primary function would be to go across the country, talk to small businessmen and organize exports for them. That kind of thing is done in the province of Ontario; perhaps the minister would not think of that. Nevertheless, that is how it ought to be done.
The activities of such a small business department could be instrumental in improving the balance of payments position of Canada. Such a department could assist Canada in establishing a more diversified pattern of trade. I am not pleased when I hear about one big sale to Yugoslavia or one big sale to Mexico. These are just one shot deals. What we need in export sales in continuing, repeat business. Earlier I talked about the sale of wheelbarrows. That is the sort of business we need, because we will sell some wheelbarrows this year, some next year and some the year after. Credit arrangements could be revolving and we could develop continuing business. As I said, what disturbs me most about some of these large sales is that they are one shot deals. This is not the kind of business that the corporation ought to go after. Sure, it looks good on the balance sheet and on the books. Sometimes the corporation lends $100 million. What we really ought to do, as I said, is develop continuing business, continuing roll-over trade. We could do that if we spent our time and effort looking after the interests of small business.
Finally, I want to repeat some of the things said by the hon. member for Scarborough East (Mr. Stackhouse), because I think they bear repeating. I think it is time for some rethinking. We must think again, not only about the government program we are presently considering, but about other government programs. It is time that we considered again the activities of this corporation. The Export Development Corporation very shortly, if this bill passes, as it may, will have $1.5 billion in circulating funds for a five-year period. The corporation is growing. Soon, a great deal of the money of Canada will be tied up in exports for five years. I suggest we must give serious consideration to a more rapid roll-over of funds. The government and the corporation must give serious consideration to borrowing money, or to allowing or encouraging private or international banks to assist in the financing of projects. Perhaps this corporation could give certain guarantees and take only a small piece of the action for itself.
We must examine our priorities whenever we examine any legislation. After all, one of the major reasons for encouraging exports is that we hope to create job opportunities for Canadians. When one looks at the fact only 43 corporations are involved, with eight corporations using 64 per cent of the money, I think it is fair to say, Mr. Speaker, that it is time we re-examined this program and reassessed its impact on jobs. Further, it is time we reexamined this program and considered it in terms of Canadian ownership. Also, it is time we re-examined the activities of this corporation in terms of the total development of Canada.
Often-I throw this thought out to the minister-credit helps in the sale of a commodity; yet, in many more cases, it is the price that counts. The foreign buyer is no different from any other buyer. He looks around to see where he can buy cheapest. It is time this government said to business in Canada, "What can we do to make business in Canada easier for businessmen; what can we do to remove the innumerable forms? How can we lower a corporate tax rate that is higher than that of any of our competitors?" Our bank rates and interest rates are higher, in many cases, than those of our competing countries.
Perhaps if we made business conditions easier for businessmen and used that $1.5 billion to cut the cost of doing business in Canada, which would reduce the total costs business must pay in Canada, we could reduce our prices on the export market. In that case perhaps we would not need to indulge in long-term credit to the extent that we now do, since our prices would be competitive. Japan, Mr. Speaker, does not rely on credit; it relies on sharp business and sharp pencils when the order books are opened. I suggest we can best develop our export trade by going out with our order books and using very, very sharp pencils. Perhaps that is the kind of approach the Export Development Corporation ought to adopt.

subsubtopic: INCREASES IN AUTHORIZED SHARE CAPITAL AND IN CEILING ON LOANS AND GUARANTEES BY CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to be able to say a few words about Bill C-3 and about the economic situation.
We have to concentrate on activity outside Canada in order to make business work inside Canada, and Canadian industries develop and progress; we have to create incentives abroad so that Canadian manufacturers can sell their products abroad.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if that really is the best solution. I believe that the prime solution is to do all in our power to give Canadian consumers exclusive rights or at least priority on Canadian products. Canadians certainly do not have such priority because they lack the means of exercising their right to priority on Canadian-made goods.
What we should be exporting, Mr. Speaker, is our surplus. What we are exporting is the main bulk of our production, and at the same time we supply safeguards to foreign companies that buy our goods, in the hope of making sure that we will sell our Canadian products.
Mr. Speaker, we are always talking about helping small industry in Canada to develop. If we are to help small and medium industries to develop, certain incentives must be found. Several incentives have been applied to help industry, and they may have helped one sector of industry, but small and medium industries have scarcely been able to take advantage of these incentives.
Mr. Speaker, small industry does not have the means of taking out loans at reasonable rates of interest.
The government was kind enough to pass legislation enabling small business to borrow $25,000 at a quite reasonable interest rate. This was appreciated by small business, but it did not contribute to assist them properly because $25,000 does not go very far. As a matter of fact,

March 14, 1973

when a businessman needs machines costing $15,000 or $18,000 each, a loan of $25,000 is not enough because he cannot enlarge his business with such a small capital.
One could say that it is still possible to resort to the Industrial Development Bank, which can doubtless help small businesses. In fact, the IDB indirectly helped small industries which cannot affort to borrow from other banks. The IDB also finds that guarantees are not satisfactory and it almost always refuses loans to small businesses. Then, the latter find themselves in a sad plight.
I suggest, in order to really assist small businesses, that we enable them to borrow up to $100,000 instead of $25,000, and at a very reasonable interest rate, such as 5 4, 6 or 6 i per cent. This would be reasonable and very much appreciated by small businesses.
Then, if we want our industries to be productive, we must enable them to do so and give them the necessary means. When they are given means to produce, they employ people who earn wages, and these industries are thus more likely to sell their products at home because the people who are working have the necessary purchasing power to buy some of the products manufactured by these small industries. There is a tax law which is detrimental to the small and medium industries. Small industry is enjoying some tax relief, but it is not sufficient to help its development in a normal way. The income tax legislation which was adopted by the 28th Parliament is greatly detrimental to small industry which is unable to hold on to its capital for development purposes.
The Industrial Development Bank is lending money at interest rates which are almost usurious, that is from 101 to 12 per cent. The smaller the enterprise, the less credit it has and the less it is in a position to pay high interest rates. So, the Industrial Development Bank is doing like all the others: exploiting the small industry through interest rates.
Furthermore, the assistance granted to small industry through all kinds of technical means is far from being sufficient because the Industrial Development Bank charges 12 per cent interest on its loans, and the small businessman must get into debt for almost $100,000 to obtain $20,000.
And after that the Industrial Development Bank takes the interests and the reimbursements are almost totally taxable. The small businessman has heavy reimbursements to make and heavy taxes to pay which puts him in a difficult situation. Quite often he is unable to pay the interest and the taxes imposed on his reimbursements in addition to his own taxes.
There is also the 12 per cent sales tax on all materials produced in Canada. The government is helping industry by simply levying a kind of indirect tax. In fact, this is not assistance but indirect taxation because if the industrialist can operate his industry for at least 4 or 5 years he will have reimbursed his total debt to the government and the balance is a net profit for the latter.
This assistance, mainly as regards small business, is not truly realistic; we could improve the situation and provide more assistance to small industries through other means.
Export Development Act
We should also adopt a tariff legislation which would better fit the reality of the current market and be tailored to our industries' needs. Until now several reviews have taken place but more remain to be done to enable Canadians to export their surplus. These factors are essential to stimulate the industries and their growth.
Mr. Speaker, 90 per cent of the grants have been paid to Canadian enterprises; in other words, 90 per cent of the small businesses still belong to Canadians. In order to maintain those small enterprises, we will have to fight still more, to make other incentives or other means available to the Canadian people to unable them to exist, because the small business owner is now going through an economic regression. As a matter of fact, there have never been so many bankruptcies. A great number of small enterprises are driven to bankruptcy, as they are unable to sell their products because those who buy them are insolvent and often go bankrupt. Those small industries have to bear the consequences of those bankruptcies.
If we are able to grant incentives so as to promote the sale of products to foreigners, we should also be able to establish some safeguards to protect Canadian industries against insolvent Canadian creditors, on account of whom astronomical sums of money are lost by small business owners and even by the government, in taxes of all kinds.
When governments have to be among creditors, when bankruptcies happen, they have to take their share of the loss as well as the others; that kind of loss is more easily assumed by governments than by small taxpayers. Now the latter would surely need appropriate measures that would give them some protection as to the sale of their products to the Canadian people; as a matter of fact, a great number of Canadians buy products for which they are unable to pay. The small business owner has to bear the burden and a chain reaction follows whereby a great number of small industries must close down.
A current regulation stipulates that the industrialist who buys $50,000 worth of machinery can obtain government loans; but if the machinery costs less than $50,000, the small industrialist cannot avail himself of the benefits offered by the government.
However, for the smaller industries, a $50,000 purchase is a lot. Many are unable to get into debt for $50,000 though they would ' need machinery. Many would buy $10,000, $12,000 or $15,000 worth of machinery a year, but they cannot afford it.
On the other hand, if government aid was more efficient and if the amount of assistance available to the small enterprise was lowered, to $5,000 from $50,000 for instance, this would mean an incentive not any costlier for the government. In fact, if it really intends to solve the unemployment problem, the government can certainly make more substantial loans available to solvent industries, a good number of which could produce valuable goods needed by Canadians or readily exportable but, on the other hand, many of them cannot develop on account of the conditions I have just mentioned.
And if we intend to maintain our economy afloat such small industries must operate at reasonable cost. If we want to sell abroad, we must come up with competitive prices, since prices govern the market. And if we fleece

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
the small or medium industries through taxes, transportation tariffs, higher gasoline prices, municipal, school and other taxes, we keep on stifling them because it is rather difficult to produce cheaply what is necessary if we want to sell. And if we want to sell at low prices, the first thing to do is to establish reasonable interest rates for industrialists.
Secondly, we must grant these industries every possible incentive, allow them to benefit from grants for instance, and lower the $5,000 minimum which may be borrowed because this measure is of no great help to a small business. And if this amount is lowered to $5,000, many small businessmen will benefit.
Thus, small businesses could produce more cheaply and governments could perhaps lower the 12 per cent tax, abolish all the taxes which boost the cost of merchandise and thus decrease their cost. If the cost of merchandise was lower, we could export much more because our prices would also be lower. In return, we could manufacture in greater quantity, which would enable us to reduce the unemployment rate and stabilize our economy.
In order to do so, we must be realistic and not consider the small businessman as an executive with all the necessary capital who can be required to pay any tax. We should not then increase prices endlessly and think that the small businessman will be able to cope no matter what.
We have all kinds of programs to help industries but it seems that almost all industries are worse off after receiving such aid than before, which means something is wrong. Other solutions must certainly be sought, and of course they must be realistic.
Mr. Speaker, we should be concerned about all those things. We are not against the bill, we are not opposed to making capital available to foreigners for the purchase of Canadian products since we want Canadians to sell as much as possible. However, we also want Canadians to be able to produce at low cost. That is one of the first aspects hon. ministers should concentrate on to find solutions.
Markets are easily found, industry can easily operate when products can be sold at low prices.
However, in the present economy of constantly increasing prices and soaring costs, it becomes very hard for small industries to compete with the big ones.
If we really want to help small industries, if we really want them to exist, we must find some sort of a corrective; we really must amend regulations and acts concerning the help to the small industry to assist it efficiently so it can prosper.
The present type of help is somewhat contrary to the facts. We are actually offering help to some foreign countries so that they can buy Canadian products, but we must not forget that if we export, we must also import. If we must import and export, it does little to improve the Canadian economy, the gross national product.
If we produce for $114 billion, Mr. Speaker, but import for $80 billion and export for the same amount, nothing is changed in the Canadian economic system. This does not alter the situation. If we want to export, it is necessary to import. And this is not a real solution. The answer is to

enable Canadians to make all possible purchases, to consume as much as possible in Canada to make our industries work. We should export surpluses in exchange for goods we are not producing. Exports should serve this purpose only. We are far from using our exports to this end.
We try to produce, to export but not to import, which becomes rather difficult because if we only sell our products without buying anything from other countries, we will not do it very long. Those countries will turn their backs on us and they will deal with other countries with which they will be able to trade.
As to foreign countries, we should trade with them to meet the essential needs of our economy and theirs.
Thus, to be logical, it is necessary to develop Canadian markets and to put the necessary purchasing power in the hands of Canadians to enable our industries to sell the biggest part of their production in Canada. It is necessary to further stimulate the production and consumption by increasing the purchasing power of taxpayers on par with the industrial and economic growth of our country.
Mr. ]ohn Harney (Scarborough West): Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) had to give up speaking sometime ago because, as he said, he was taken with a rather bad cold and his voice gave way. I would like to suggest that he was not being absolutely true to fact, because I suspect that he was moved to the point of choking by the admiration he had when it came to the prospect of the beautiful co-ordination that existed between the centres of high finance in this country and the directors of this corporation as indicated by a reading of the Export Development Corporation report. I am quite sure that is really what happened to him. He was choked with emotion when he looked at the startling involvement of this corporation. Following upon that was the information given to us by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn), who was looking at the beautiful pictures contained in this report.
This is indeed a very handsome report, loaded with coloured pictures, not only of members of the board, but with those which give us some idea of projects reportedly supported by the Export Development Corporation. For example, on page 11 is a picture of a beautiful seaside resort, something which would tempt members of this House today. In the background we have palm trees, and girls walking beside the pool, and it has the following caption:
Interest in tourist facilities in the Caribbean is very high among Canadian investors. One third of the inquiries received for EDC Foreign Investment Insurance are for investments to be made in that part of the world.
This is very interesting when we consider the kind of concern presented a few days ago by church leaders in Canada asking for participation in the development of under-developed countries. It is surprising that this is the kind of project in respect of which the EDC is receiving inquiries.
However, let us remember that these inquiries received by the EDC are in respect of foreign investment insurance
March 14, 1973

rather than loans. There is a clause in the act controlling the EDC which allows that corporation to provide insurance to Canadian investors who want to invest abroad in areas which may not be entirely stable. As a matter of fact, I think the act specifies areas in which there may be revolution, riot and war. If, rather than assisting underdeveloped countries in very great need of basic industry and other development, Canadian investors show interest in areas of the kind pictured at page 11, then we may expect war, riot and other civil disturbances.
Let me look at other pictures in this booklet that are very handsome, indeed. On page 26, we have a picture of a more serious nature. It is a picture of a pulp mill, specifically a kraft pulpmill in New Zealand. The caption reads:
EDC made a $10.3 million loan to cover the sale of Canadian services and equipment for expansion of a kraft pulpmill and newsprint project in New Zealand. The EDC financing covered 90 per cent of the export value of the sale.
It seems to me that one of the rationales of the EDC is the creation of jobs in Canada. I have travelled around this country and have seen some kraft pulp mills. It might occur to some of us, or indeed some of those in the EDC, that this is an industry in Canada in which jobs could be eliminated by designing these pulp mills in such a way they can produce the products overseas. We can eliminate jobs in Canada in these pulp mills. In this situation, may we not be allowed to ask ourselves if, by the practices adopted by the government of this country, we are not contributing to a state in Canada which in fact helps the foreign corporation?
Let me come back to the point of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville. He was referring to the directors of the corporation. One is allowed to wonder, if not suspect, that there might be some kind of co-ordination. I do not say collusion, between directors of the Export Development Corporation and directors of large corporations in Canada. I was particularly interested in one picture, and I am looking at the picture of Mr. P. R. Sandwell, who is a director of the corporation and chairman of the board of Sandwell and Co. Limited, particularly when we connect him with others in the list of loans by the EDC.
Let me refer briefly to a publication called Canadian Pulp and Paper Industry which has linked Mr. Simons with Mr. Sandwell. You will see that he is associated there with H. A. Simons (International) Ltd. which was financed in respect of pulp mill equipment, and consulting and supervisory engineering services, for a project in Argentina to the extent of $12 million. Simons and Sandwell have been linked in the past as having been responsible for the engineering and design of about one-third of the paper mills built in the world since 1945. Let me quote from Canadian Pulp and Paper Industry:
"Worldwide, they know of Simons and Sandwell."
I suggest they also know of Simons and Sandwell in Ottawa. I do not want to dwell on this aspect because it may not be exactly surprising. The aspect of the Export Development Corporation on which I should like to dwell is the aspect concerning the kinds of loans and to what kinds of countries these loans are directed.
Export Development Act
I wish I had before me the report of the Export Development Corporation for 1972. As you know, Mr. Speaker, reports come late, so we must go to other sources for more current information. In the Globe and Mail in December there was buried in the business pages a little item which I should like to read. It states:
The Canadian Export Development Corporation will lend Brazil. ..
Note it states will lend "Brazil".
. . . $26.5 million to help that country buy electrical equipment in Canada.
"The corporation said the money will be loaned to Light-servigos de electricidade SA. Rio de Janeiro, a private Brazilian utility company.
"The loan is guaranteed by the government of Brazil. "Light-services must buy at least $23 million worth of transmission and distribution equipment from such companies as Canadian General Electric, Collins Radio, Westinghouse Canada, Canadian Marconi and others under the agreement."
You will notice that all of these companies are Canadian because they somehow have the name "Canada" or "Canadian" and we can therefore believe they are Canadian companies. But, let us note the first sentence which states:
The Canadian Export Development Corporation will lend Brazil $26.5 million to help that country buy electrical equipment in Canada.
However, if we look more closely at the transaction we do not find that the Export Development Corporation is lending Brazil, specifically, a sum of $26.5 million but is to lend it to Light-servigos of Brazil. What kind of a corporation or a company is Light-servigos which is known, by the way, in Brazil simply as Light. The Portugese name of this company covers a firm which is owned to the extent of 83 per cent by Brascan, a massive company controlled in Canada although the majority of its shares are held in the United States. We have an inkling now of what is really happening. What appears at first to be a loan to a country in need of development money that it may buy our Canadian products turns out to be a loan to a private company. Then, we discover that that private company in turn is owned by a rather large Canadian company, a rather well-known company, which has acted from time to time in the past as a farm club for putative Liberal cabinet ministers, or vice versa for Brazilian Traction directors.
So far we are beginning to receive some information which is of value to us. However, the thought of Canadian money going to Brazil still might strike some compassionate hearts as a good thing because Brazil is a country which is in need of development. Let us look at the social development there has been in Brazil over the past ten years. There is a certain gentleman named McNamara who could not be counted as one of the world's subversives, a friend of the late President Kennedy, who now, I think, is involved in an institution called the World Bank. He noted that in Brazil the richest 5 per cent of the population saw its share of the national income rise during the 1960's from 29 per cent to 38 per cent, while the poorest 40 per cent saw its share drop from 10 per cent to 8 per cent. I know that we cannot make a direct connection between Canadian activity in Brazil and what is going on internally in that country, but it should be obvi-

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
ous to us that our activities in lending money to a private company in Brazil, which in turn is owned by a Canadian company, are not necessarily helping out in respect of the problem of social equalization in Brazil.
I could mention a number of other countries to which the Export Development Corporation directs its largesse. I think if we added up all these countries we would not be able to put many of them in the list of the world's progressive, democratic nations. However, I can speak on that point at another time. There is another aspect of the Export Development Corporation with which I should like to deal, apart from its being a branch of our own Canadian imperialism. I refer to its function in carrying out our role as a nation in helping out the underdeveloped parts of the world. We have several entities in this country which appear to direct their interests to trade and to aid with the under-developed parts of the world. Several of these entities are government or government-controlled or government-owned entities.
Indeed, a few years ago there was a certain amount of concern in the cabinet of the time about co-ordinating the activities of these various entities because it appeared that some of them could be working at cross purposes. There was what I think was called an interdepartmental committee structured to bring all the external activities of the Canadian government together so that they could be coordinated. To give an idea of what was involved here, there was some consideration, for example, given to coordinating the activities of the Canadian International Development Agency with that of the Export Development Corporation because both agencies are involved in the matter of economic aid and economic assistance, as I believe it is called.
I shall give an example of the amount of involvement of CIDA. I have the report for 1970-71 of the Canadian International Development Agency before me. In a column at page 10 entitled "Appropriations and Authorizations" for 1971-72, we find these appropriations and authorizations broken into two major parts. First of all, we have appropriations and authorizations to multilateral agencies in such matters as international emergency relief and food aid. The total of these multilateral contributions is some $204 million, which is a respectable amount by world standards. Multilateral contributions are broken down fairly extensively later on in the publication in other columns. Below that, however, we have a second section which deals with bilateral assistance and there are two items: technical assistance in an amount of $43 million and economic assistance in an amount of $178.8 million. That is a large amount of money.
As a matter of fact the bilateral total, talking about economic assistance, amounting to $221.8 million exceeds the total of the non-bilateral contribution of $204.6 million. Even in terms of the amount we are talking about for the Export Development Corporation which has of course, a limitation on its lending capacity which is not what it will lend in any one year, we realize that this figure is indeed very large. The activities of CIDA in large measure are very much like the kind of activities in which the Export Development Corporation is supposed to be involved.

If we hesitate to believe that this is the case, we have the recent word of the president of the Canadian Export Development Corporation, Mr. Paul Gerin-Lajoie. I quote from an article which recently appeared in one of the newspapers in Canada, the Globe and Mail. I see it is a CP article so every newspaper carried it. It reads:
Paul Gerin-Lajoie, president of the Canadian International Development Agency, told the Montreal Board of Trade yesterday that "particular Canadian business enterprises would find it difficult if not impossible to remain economically viable without the purchases CIDA makes from them".
He goes on to point out exactly what CIDA has been able to do in order to help Canadian business. Indeed, he goes on to chide Canadian businessmen for not being as ready as they could be to trade with the third world, particularly the developing world. I will not go on to quote any more from Mr. Gerin-Lajoie because I think the point has been made that this CIDA function is very much like the function of the Export Development Corporation. If the EDC is designed to increase industrial expansion in Canada by increasing industrial expansion abroad, that is fine, I suppose, because it is working within its terms of reference, but we really should wonder whether CIDA is working within its terms of reference or indeed whether or not both corporations are working to those kinds of ends that are so often mentioned in speeches that come from cabinet ministers, especially when they are out of the House, ends that have to do with aid to developing countries.
I am sure that many heads in cabinet nodded with agreement, not with sleep, when they were addressed in these terms by the churchmen of Canada the other day. I quote from their brief as follows:
Today, there is a growing resistance against the economic growth model for development in the third world. Several developing countries are increasingly resisting the pressures of modern industrialization, especially where the cost is another form of economic colonization and dependence.
I suggested a while ago that a lot of the effort of the Export Development Corporation is our own form of Canadian imperialism in the third world. The brief goes on to read:
The realities of this resistance force all of us in the western industrial countries to critically re-examine our models for development. The third world resistance is telling us that the human cost of the economic growth model is too high. As an alternative, the third world is advocating development models based on the goal of balanced growth with an equitable distribution of income across the board.
So, if we are to co-ordinate our external economic activity, what we really should do is, first, bring the various entities, such as the EDC and CIDA, under one roof and preferably not under a Crown corporation roof, rather under the control of one minister so that we in the House can actively criticize the programs of these agencies. It is all very well to say that we are given reports with very pretty pictures indeed, but in most cases we have no idea from these reports exactly what the nature of these foreign involvements is and what these loans amount to.
For example, one of our agencies will tell us very religiously, as they do in the estimates for this year, exactly what kinds of grants and contributions to multilateral and
March 14, 1973

international assistance programs they are making. We can read down the list and find, for example, that we propose this year to give to the Society for International Development $5,000. It is herewith listed so that all members of this parliament and indeed the citizens of Canada can know exactly where our international development aid is going. But if we look on the same page, we find under grants for economic and technical assistance, $144,340,000 with no specification whatsoever, no clue at all as to where this money is going.
So, when it comes to aid, we can go over the program with a magnifying glass and we can question every detail. We know exactly what little church in what country is getting whatever bit of money to buy food. But when it comes to economic assistance, all we are given are lump sums without detail. We are not given details, we are given flossy reports with multi-coloured pictures but no breakdown of wliat the purpose of the economic assistance is or exactly to what kind of venture it is going. I think in the near future we should seek to bring together under one roof, as I suggested, all our external programs, programs of aid and of economic assistance and programs involving loans to foreign countries or foreign corporations, which in turn perhaps are simply corporations in Canada whether they be foreign or Canadian owned. Second, what we need is much more detail so that we know what is going on.
I should like now to go back to the report for 1971 of the Export Development Corporation. On pages 23 and 24, there is a listing of the countries and of the borrowers within those countries who have been helped by the Export Development Corporation, a list of the products, finance, exporting in Canada, date of contract, repayment terms, amount of financing, and so on. Some sums amount to $12 million, others to $9 million, one to the Union des Transports Aeriens in France for $2,700,000, and to the President of India $1,500,000. But then, at the end of page 24, under section 31 of the Export Development Act it says: "to the Imperial government of Iran, products to be financed". What are they? Various. What exporter? Various Canadian suppliers. What is the amount? $100 million. What other details? None. So what kind of scrutiny can we give this program in the House when we are only given such scanty information? One thing I can say now is that when this matter comes to committee we will expect to see just what kind of detail is available for members of the House.
There is another aspect of the export development program that we should consider. Where exactly in Canada are these exports produced? It is a very important question, because we have spent several hundreds of millions of dollars over the past few years to rid ourselves of the problem of economic disparity in Canada-I should say, "in order to rid ourselves" because we have not done it yet. The ministry in charge of that program is a little stunned right now because all the money it has spent over the past few years has not brought about the result that was expected; indeed, regional disparity is still with us. But this parliament went into the program in good faith because it believed that it was essential for reasons of natural and social justice, and essential for the principle of Canadian unity, that the wealth and productivity of this
Export Development Act
country should be directed equally to satisfy the needs of all sectors of the country.
We have here the Export Development Corporation. In the 1960's it dished out some $800 million-a fairly sizeable sum. Were these $800 million spent evenly across Canada with some respect for the needs of the less developed regions of our country? Not at all. Of the $800 million, $650 million went to Ontario and Quebec. I wish I had the breakdown for the two provinces because I suspect that the lion's share of the $650 million went to Ontario which is more in a position to take advantage of this kind of largesse than the province of Quebec. Here we have an aspect of our government in Canada acting at cross purposes with a ministerial program called DREE. We can call the Export Development Corporation our contra-DREE program or anti-DREE program. I tried to reverse or juggle the letters around a few days ago and I came up with EERD, and I only wish I could find some way of putting "W" in front, because then we would have something very telling and informative, for certainly something "WEERD" is going on here.
In this parliament we do not have a real understanding of what our economic ventures and economic activities add up to, and there are several accounts under which we could challenge the worth of the program of the Export Development Corporation. I know that some of my colleagues to my right dwelt at some length on the fact that multinational corporations were involved as recipients of the largesse of the Export Development Corporation. However, if you do not mind, Mr. Speaker, I will add just one more element. It is not even my own. It comes from the brief presented by the church leaders to the cabinet the other day, and I quote:
It is becoming increasingly evident that multinational corporations are having a dominant impact on development planning and trade patterns. We are acutely aware of this problem since Canada is a country with a large percentage of foreign control. This trend must be counterbalanced by other measures. For example, could the Canadian government expand our public importing systems in order to encourage imports from those countries that lack the sophisticated marketing systems of the giant corporations?
Let us talk for a moment about imports as well as exports. It is useless to pretend that we can only be dealing with exports in this world where import from and export from must be a two-way street.
I come back again to that country to which I referred a while ago, to look at our activities in terms of import and export trade between Canada and Brazil. For example, in 1970 imports to Canada from Brazil amounted to $49.3 million. Exports from Canada to Brazil in 1970 amounted to $87.4 million. Certainly next year, by the time Brascan gets its assistance from the EDC, exports from Canada to Brazil will be in even larger imbalance than the imports we get from that country.
You see, what we are doing essentially with the EDC is dealing with the top tenth of the world's industrial activity. We are doing almost nothing with that nine-tenths of the world that is submerged out of reach of that industrial activity, and not only out of reach of that activity, but out of reach of the benefits that come from it. So how can we, when it comes to speech-making time here, the equivalent

March 14, 1973
Export Development Act
of convocation time in university, stand up and make all these beautiful speeches about how we are out to help develop the underdeveloped world, when all we are doing is simply shoring-up the kind of industrial enterprise which suits the industrial giants of this country. We do nothing effective, in real and lasting terms, to help the third world, and those parts of the third world that are sorely affected, to pull themselves up from the economic desperation in which they find themselves?
I will end fairly soon, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure some people will be glad to hear that. But there is one point I wish to make now. It is not a particularly new point, but it is a point worthwhile making over and over again. What we have here really in the efforts and activities of the EDC is a sample of that very old capitalist technique- there, I have used the word-of running to government to get cheap money, of running to government to insure the risks when it is rather difficult or rather expensive to get money for investment on the normal investment market, or when there are no insurance companies that will take the risks, simply because they are bad or chancy risks.
This has always worked very well for those who understand the nature of the capitalist system. As economist Frank Park put it some years ago:
The ingenious idea was to finance on government advances and on the sale of government-guaranteed bonds while the promoting group kept all the common stock (absolute ownership and control) in return for 'services rendered.'
That is an ancient principle, and it has always worked very well for that sector of our economy which is in definite control of the economy as a whole. Here again we have the same procedures going on. Brazilian Traction-I am sorry, it is now called Brascan, that is its new avatar, but it is still the old Brazilian Traction-rather than going out on the market to borrow money at the going rates gets a loan, indirectly mind you, from the Export Development
Corporation at very good rates indeed, at 6 per cent or 7 per cent. With this loan, it can develop the capitalization it needs in Brazil, and can carry on its form of imperialism, and bring back very good dividends to its Canadian as well as American shareholders. And we, the people of Canada, have taken the risk, but we have none of the control.
You know, Mr. Speaker, in most of the provinces in this country we do not let private interests control the development of hydroelectric power. Even Conservative Ontario many years ago adopted the principle that the development of hydroelectric power should be in public hands. As a matter of fact, private development of hydro-electric power cannot be undertaken very much more in Canada, although it was done in the case of Churchill Falls a few years ago. But we allow and encourage our Canadian companies to go and do it elsewhere, and we, the public, take on the capitalization and all the risks,' while they make the profits.
Just recently there was an announcement to the effect that the British Columbia government would get into some kind of joint enterprise with Brascan to develop resources in northern British Columbia. But at least the British Columbia government had the wisdom to say, "For our part of the investment we want joint control. We want a piece of the action so that the people of British Columbia can get part of the return." Now, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to be involved in foreign enterprises could we not ask that the people of Canada get a piece of the action, get a piece of the control? Mr. Speaker, I notice that you are about to rise from your chair, and if you are going to call it six o'clock, may I do it for you?
